Title: Zelensky acknowledges Ukraine did not coordinate Libya strike with European partners

President Volodymyr Zelensky acknowledged on Nov. 27 that Ukraine had not coordinated its recent naval strike on Russian ships in Libya with European partners, after Italian officials publicly disputed his earlier claims.

"I spoke with Giorgia Meloni today. We discussed the issues we are working on, and it is important that we understand each other. I confirmed that the recent operation in Libya was carried out without prior coordination with our European partners," Zelensky said following a phone call with the Italian prime minister.

The clarification came hours after Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani rejected Zelensky's earlier statements regarding coordination with allies.

"None of us were informed, nobody knew anything about what the Ukrainians were doing in Libya. So what Zelensky said is not true," Tajani said in an interview with Sky TG24.

Speaking in an interview with the BBC published on Nov. 26, Zelensky had said Ukrainian diplomats work with their foreign counterparts whenever Ukrainian forces operate in foreign or international waters or near another country's infrastructure.

"Our forces never attack without any coordination with other partners," Zelensky said.

Ukraine has been expanding the reach of its strikes on Russian military assets, hitting targets in the Baltic, Black, and Mediterranean seas over the past week, potentially signaling a shift in Kyiv's strategy to undermine Russia's war machine, while raising concerns among some European partners over the risk of escalation.

Ukrainian naval drones struck the Russian Navy corvette Merkury at the port of Benghazi in Libya on Nov. 22. The operation was carried out by Ukrainian forces in coordination with the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), using seven domestically produced naval drones.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni earlier cautioned against the war spilling over into the Mediterranean following Ukraine's strikes on Russian vessels in the Libyan port of Benghazi.

On Nov. 17, a Ukrainian missile strike caused an entire section of the Crimean Bridge to collapse.

Days later, Ukraine struck the sanctioned Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland, while explosions were reported near Russia's Baltic Fleet base in Kaliningrad Oblast.

Ukraine has not commented on the incident in Kaliningrad.

Title: Ukraine war latest: Ukraine hits missile fuel production facility in Russia's Tula Oblast, military says
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/ukraine-war-latest-ukraine-hits-missile-fuel-production-facility-in-russias-tula-oblast-military-says

**Key developments on Nov. 27:**

- Ukraine hits missile fuel production facility in Russia's Tula Oblast, military says
- Starshield speed restrictions apply only to Russian-occupied territories, hamper Ukraine's middle strike campaign, military sources say
- Ukraine's Azov announces 'Hell-3' operation, destroys Russian fuel depot in occupied Donetsk Oblast
- 9 Ukrainian children returned from Russian-occupied territories, Russia through Melania Trump's mediation, Zelensky says

Ukraine targeted a Russian facility involved in producing solid rocket fuel, striking the Efremov Synthetic Rubber Plant in Tula Oblast overnight on Nov. 27, the General Staff confirmed.

The operation was carried out by Ukrainian forces in cooperation with the Black Spark ("Chornaya Iskra" in Russian) resistance movement operating in Russia, the General Staff said.

Synthetic rubber is a key component of solid rocket fuel, and the plant manufactures fuel used in Iskander ballistic missiles, according to the General Staff.

"Without it, the Iskander is just a piece of metal sitting in storage. These are the very missiles Russia's army uses to strike Ukrainian cities, energy infrastructure, and civilian targets," the General Staff said.

The full extent of the damage is still being assessed, the General Staff added.

In a statement on Nov. 27, the General Staff also confirmed a strike on the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery in Russia's Rostov Oblast, which has an annual processing capacity of up to 7.5 million metric tons of oil. The strike destroyed 20 horizontal storage tanks and damaged another 21 horizontal tanks, 11 vertical tanks, and a section of pipeline.

## `Starshield speed restrictions apply only to Russian-occupied territories, hamper Ukraine's middle strike campaign, military sources say`

Speed restrictions on the U.S.-provided Starshield satellite communications system are hampering Ukrainian strike drone operations in Russian-occupied territory, leading to heavy drone losses and forcing the military to cancel some missions, two Ukrainian military sources told the Kyiv Independent on Nov. 27.

The restrictions, first introduced in October, have added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington over U.S. military and political support for Ukraine, while undermining Ukraine's ability to both strike Russian targets and defend against aerial attacks.

"The speed restrictions on Starshield only exist over territory of Ukraine that is temporarily occupied by Russia," a senior member of the Ukrainian military told the Kyiv Independent.

"There has clearly been a political decision to hamper the system's function over areas Russia currently controls."

Another member of the Ukrainian military told the Kyiv Independent that the restrictions have significantly affected Ukraine's medium-range strike drones, including the Fire Point FP-2, which can carry a payload of up to 200 kilograms (440 pounds) and has a range of up to 700 kilometers (435 miles).

The restrictions have resulted in extremely high drone losses during some strike missions, while others have been canceled altogether, the source said.

## `Ukraine's Azov announces 'Hell-3' operation, destroys Russian fuel depot in occupied Donetsk Oblast`

Azov's 1st Corps and the 9th Army Corps announced the success of operation "Hell-3," saying they had destroyed Russian fuel reserves concealed in Russian-occupied Donetsk Oblast.

Russian forces had concealed the fuel depot and attempted to protect it with camouflage, electronic warfare systems and mobile fire groups, but the Ukrainian units managed to destroy both the storage site and its supporting logistics infrastructure, Azov said.

The two previous phases also targeted Russian storage and logistics infrastructure in occupied Ukrainian territory.

On Aug. 17, Azov announced Operation Hell-2 targeting Russian fuel infrastructure across occupied Donetsk Oblast. The corps said it destroyed 67 fuel tanks containing a total of 4,221 metric tons of fuel, as well as vehicles used to transport supplies to Russian troops.

Operation Hell-1, announced on July 1, struck a major Russian fuel depot in Novoamvrosiivka, occupied Donetsk Oblast, using Hornet drones. The multi-stage operation also targeted railway infrastructure supplying the facility, an electrical substation, and fuel storage tanks, eventually forcing Russian forces to abandon the depot and redirect supplies into Russia, Azov said.

## `9 Ukrainian children returned from Russian-occupied territories, Russia through Melania Trump's mediation, Zelensky says`

Nine Ukrainian children have returned to Ukraine from Russian-occupied territories and Russia through the mediation of U.S. first lady Melania Trump, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Nov. 27 on X.

Those who returned also included a grandmother who accompanied her grandson and a girl named Anastasiia, who is a resident of a children's residential institution in the town of Oleshky in the Russian-occupied part of Kherson.

Zelensky said the children were brought back from Russian-occupied Crimea, as well as parts of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts.

The youngest child among those returned was eight years old, according to Zelensky.

The president thanked Melania Trump for her assistance and mediation, as well as Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, the Bring Kids Back UA initiative, and international partners.

According to Zelensky, Ukraine has secured the return of 2,875 children, though the president did not specify the timeframe.

"We remember everyone. We are doing everything possible to find them and bring them back to their families and loved ones," Zelensky said.

Title: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3pw4yrr8kz9o

<article (part 1 of 2)>
**Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.**

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

## Surviving blackouts

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

## Raving through the war

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch \[a famously delicious soup made of beetroot\] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

## How does it all end?

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

Title: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3pw4yrr8kz9o

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

Title: Germany votes through nearly 12 billion euros in Ukraine support for 2027
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/germany-votes-through-nearly-12-billion-euros-in-ukraine-support-for-2027

<article>
The German Parliament approved 11.6 billion euros ($12.7 billion) in support for Ukraine as part of the country's 2027 budget, which was voted through on Nov. 27.

President Volodymyr Zelensky identified a 70 billion euro ($77 billion) hole in Ukraine's finances for 2027, and Kyiv is counting on partners to cover that gap, and fast.

Failure to do so would mean the International Monetary Fund cannot continue its support for Ukraine, which requires Kyiv to have a sound budget, the EU's Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis told the Kyiv Independent.

Negotiations are ongoing for the EU to agree a 45 billion euro ($49 billion) loan by the end of 2027, but that still leaves 25 billion euros ($27 billion) for Ukraine's allies to find and provide — and fast.

Germany's new budget, now approved by the parliament in Berlin, will bridge almost half of that shortfall on its own.

The final draft of the budget partially breaks down the 11.6 billion, but the largest share, titled simply "Ukraine support," already accounts for 9 billion ($10 billion) of the total.

Also listed in the budget are smaller amounts for capacity building within Ukraine's government, specifically in the defense and foreign ministries, plus 25 million euros ($27 million) earmarked for the medical treatment of Ukrainian soldiers.

Germany has also earmarked 649 million euros ($710 million) for the European Peace Facility (EPF), an EU pot of money funded directly by member-state contributions, which can be used to procure weapons for Ukraine.

A week earlier, EU countries agreed to provide 1 billion euros in military support for Ukraine by drawing from the EPF.

Germany is the third-largest donor to Ukraine since Russia initiated its full-scale invasion in 2022, behind only the U.S. and the EU, according to data compiled by the Kiel Institute.

And Chancellor Friedrich Merz is one of the loudest voices pushing for the EU to agree on longer-term financial support for Ukraine by the end of the year, backed by all 27 member states with no opt-outs.
</article>

Title: Russian soldier who was 13 when Russia launched full-scale invasion killed in Ukraine, media reports

<article>
An 18-year-old Russian soldier who was just 13 when Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 has been killed in the war, independent Russian outlet Mediazona reported on Nov. 27.

Danil Kurlenya, from the town of Bolotnoye in Russia’s Novosibirsk Oblast, was reportedly killed on Nov. 11, according to a memorial post on the Russian social media platform VKontakte, first discovered by the Telegram channel Goryushko, which tracks Russian military deaths.

The Kyiv Independent can't immediately verify this claim.

Born on May 21, 2008, Kurlenya is the first known Russian soldier killed in Ukraine who was born during the presidency of Dmitry Medvedev, who led Russia from 2008 to 2012. Medvedev was the only person other than Vladimir Putin to serve as Russia's president since 2000, when Putin first took office.

Mediazona also found that Kurlenya was registered on the website of Movement of the First, a pro-Kremlin Russian youth organization.

It remains unclear when or how he joined the Russian military or where exactly he was killed.

His death comes as Russia continues to suffer heavy casualties in its nearly five-year-long full-scale war against Ukraine.

Earlier in November, Mediazona estimated that around 700,000 Russian soldiers have likely been killed in Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine as of September 2026, citing the analysis of recently leaked data from Rosstat, country's state statistics agency.

Mediazona, together with the BBC's Russian Service, has since May 2022 run one of the only verified counts of Russian war deaths, building a database of confirmed cases from social media posts, pictures of graves, and other official or organic sources. As of early November, the count stood at 285,881.

In a major development in tracking Russian losses, hacker groups Belarusian Cyberpartisans and Silent Crow claimed responsibility on Nov. 7 for a cyberattack on Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).

The hackers leaked death records indicating that between 394,000 and 450,000 people fighting on Russia's side, or otherwise linked to the war, had died since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Title: 'Normal staffing issue' — IAEA chief dismisses criticism over appointment of sanctioned Russian as deputy

<article>
The International Atomic Energy Agency's (IAEA) director general, Rafael Grossi, responded to criticism over his appointment of a Russian official to the second highest-ranking role at the international organization, calling the decision a "normal staffing issue" on Nov. 27.

"In appointing a person, I am not appointing a policy, I am not rewarding a country," Grossi told BBC News, according to excerpts shared with the Kyiv Independent.

"International organisations are staffed with people from different countries who have different kinds of expertise. He is occupying a position which was occupied in the past by another Russian and there was no public outcry about that. This is a normal staffing issue," Grossi added.

The official in question, Alexey Ferapontov, serves as the deputy head of the Russian Federal Service for Environmental, Technological and Nuclear Supervision (Rostekhnadzor).

Ferapontov was sanctioned by Ukraine in February 2023 over his role in "legitimizing the illegal seizure of the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) and extending Russian regulatory control over it," according to Ukraine's **Foreign Ministry**.

"International civil servants are totally independent, as per UN's Charter," Grossi said. "I can understand in an atmosphere of a war, people may have these kinds of observations," he added, noting that the IAEA has "all types of people and all nationalities represented."

The **ZNPP,** located in the city of Enerhodar in southern Ukraine, is Europe's largest nuclear power plant. It has been under Russian occupation since the start of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine. While Moscow controls the plant and large parts of **Zaporizhzhia Oblast**, the regional capital of Zaporizhzhia and most of the oblast's population remain under Ukrainian administration.

In response to the appointment, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha branded Ferapontov's appointment as deputy director general "absurd," and described Ferapontov as "an accomplice in one of the greatest threats and gravest crimes against nuclear safety," in a social media **post**.

The EU also criticized the appointment as part of "Russia's attempt to normalize its image by trying to rejoin international fora," in comments provided to the Kyiv Independent.

That approach, "does not work," the EU's foreign affairs spokesperson Christian Wigand previously told the Kyiv Independent. "We regret the appointment."

**Grossi's plan** to appoint Ferapontov came days after nuclear safety regulators from 38 countries **warned** that Russian attacks were increasing the risk of a nuclear accident in Ukraine this coming winter.

Grossi, a candidate for U.N. Secretary-General, has served as a controversial figure as the head of the IAEA amid Russia's control of the ZNPP.

In response to news of the appointment, activist organization Greenpeace International **issued a letter** to the IAEA board calling on Grossi to immediately abandon the plans, which the organization tied as a potential conflict of interest to Grossi's campaign for the U.N.'s top post.

Greenpeace said its letter expressed "serious concern about Russia's possible leverage over the IAEA Director General, who needs the Russian government's support for his candidacy for the next U.N. Secretary-General."

Title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,650,986 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/general-staff-russia-has-lost-1-650-986-troops-in-ukraine-since-feb-24-2022

<article>
Russia has lost 1,650,986 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Nov. 28.

The number includes 2,825 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.

According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,517 tanks, 26,038 armored combat vehicles, 181,327 vehicles and fuel tanks, 52,900 artillery systems, 2,312 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,782 air defense systems, 456 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,253 unmanned ground vehicles, 36 ships and boats, and two submarines.

Russian battlefield losses have been especially heavy in recent months. October 2026 was the deadliest month for Russian troops since the start of the full-scale invasion, with 54,400 personnel killed, wounded, or missing, according to Ukraine's General Staff.

The losses continued to mount in November, with Russia losing 2,980 troops in a single day on Nov. 8 — the highest daily figure reported since February 2022, the General Staff said on Nov. 9.

Russian independent media outlet Mediazona said on Nov. 23 that around 700,000 Russian soldiers had been killed in the war, citing its analysis of recently leaked data from Rosstat, Russia's state statistics agency.

Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."

A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.

While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.

The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Title: Ukraine reportedly launches massive attack on Moscow Oblast with 460 drones

Ukraine launched a large-scale drone attack on Moscow overnight on Nov. 28, disrupting air traffic and forcing airports to close, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.

At around 11 p.m. local time on Nov. 27, Sobyanin reported that Russian forces had shot down 11 drones heading toward the Russian capital. The following morning, the mayor said that 460 drones had targeted Moscow Oblast overnight, 123 of which were intercepted en route to Moscow.

Sobyanin did not specify how many drones had been shot down across the region in total.

Ukraine had not commented on the reported attack on Moscow Oblast at the time of publication.

The reported Ukrainian attack prompted flight restrictions at several airports, including Vnukovo and Domodedovo in Moscow Oblast.

No flight restrictions were reported at another Moscow airport, Sheremetyevo. Yet the Russian media outlet Ostorozhno, Novosti, citing a passenger on a Rossiya Airlines flight from Moscow to Vladivostok, reported that the flight had not yet departed from Sheremetyevo.

Beyond Moscow, flight restrictions were also introduced at airports in Kaluga, Penza, Saratov, and Tambov, according to Russian independent media Astra.

According to Russia's Defense Ministry, Russian forces intercepted 1,246 Ukrainian drones overnight on Nov. 28 over 14 Russian regions, the Republic of Bashkortostan, and Russian-occupied Crimea.

Throughout 2026, Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range drone campaign against Russia, increasingly targeting Moscow and other regions across the country.

On the night of Nov. 16, Ukraine launched a massive drone attack on Russia, with Russian air defenses claiming to have intercepted 1,336 drones, according to Russia's Defense Ministry. The following night, the ministry reported shooting down another 1,441 Ukrainian drones.

During the same overnight period, Ukrainian forces also attacked the Crimean Bridge, destroying one of the arches used by road traffic. The bridge's railway section remains operational.

Title: Ukraine commemorates victims of Holodomor famine
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/ukraine-commemorates-victims-of-holodomor-famine

<article>
Ukraine marks the Day of Remembrance of the Victims of the Holodomor on the fourth Saturday of November each year, which falls on Nov. 28 in 2026.

Ukraine experienced three major famines in the 20th century: in 1921-1923, 1932-1933, and 1946-1947. The 1932-1933 famine was the deadliest and has been recognized by Ukraine and some other countries as a genocide of the Ukrainian people carried out by the government of Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin.

The Holodomor was preceded by the forced collectivization of farms and a campaign known as "dekulakization" — mass repression, property confiscation, and deportations targeting relatively wealthy and independent peasants, known as "kulaks," and their families.

Soviet authorities confiscated the grain Ukrainian farmers had grown, then stripped them of their remaining food supplies through numerous "in-kind fines" and searches of their homes. In December 1932, food trade was banned in 82 districts of Ukraine, while supplies of manufactured goods were also halted.

The 22-month famine claimed approximately 4 million lives in Ukraine, according to official Ukrainian figures. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance said children were particularly hard-hit by the famine. In September 1933, nearly two-thirds of schoolchildren did not return to their classrooms.

The regions hardest hit by the famine included Poltava, Cherkasy, Kirovohrad, and Kyiv.

For decades, the Holodomor remained a taboo subject. Under communist rule, even discussing the famine was strictly forbidden. Research into the tragedy began only in the late 1980s.

On this day, Ukrainians traditionally light candles in their homes in memory of those who died in the man-made famine. A nationwide minute of silence is observed at 4 p.m., and commemorative events are held across the country.
</article>

Title: Hungary reportedly lifts entry ban on Ukraine's drone forces commander
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/hungary-reportedly-lifts-entry-ban-on-ukraines-drone-forces-commander

<article>
Hungary has lifted a three-year ban on entry and residence for Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, Hungarian outlet Magyar Hang reported on Nov. 27.

The ban, which also applied across the Schengen Area, was imposed in August 2025 by then-Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto after Ukraine struck the Druzhba oil pipeline, through which Hungary received Russian oil. The move came amid tensions between Ukraine and then Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who cultivated closer ties with Russia.

Hungarian authorities linked the strike to Brovdi, who was born in Uzhhorod in western Ukraine and is ethnically Hungarian. Brovdi is the highest-ranking ethnic Hungarian serving in the Ukrainian Armed Forces.

In the April parliamentary election, Orban was defeated by Peter Magyar's party, and Magyar became Hungary's prime minister. He has adopted a more pro-Ukrainian stance than Orban, although his support for Kyiv is not unconditional.

According to Magyar Hang, the ban has now been removed from Hungary's immigration registry.

Hungary's Interior Ministry previously said the ban could be lifted if the threat to national security no longer existed. The decision to revoke it was made before Hungarian Prime Minister Magyar met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Zakarpattia Oblast.

The Nov. 24 meeting was the first between the two leaders since Magyar took office as prime minister in April. During the talks, the sides agreed to cooperate in the areas of energy, infrastructure, trade, and humanitarian affairs.
</article>

Title: Russian drones target critical infrastructure in Kyiv, residential building in Kharkiv
URL: https://kyivindependent.com/russian-drones-target-critical-infrastructure-in-kyiv-residential-building-in-kharkiv

<article>
Russian forces struck Kyiv and Kharkiv on Nov. 28, targeting critical infrastructure in the capital and hitting a residential high-rise in Ukraine's second-largest city, local authorities said.

Around noon, Russia launched drones toward several regions of Ukraine, including jet-powered ones, which are harder to intercept because of their speed and flight trajectory.

At 1:45 p.m. local time, Kyiv Independent reporters heard the first explosion in the capital following an air raid alert. Another explosion was heard about an hour later.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a critical infrastructure facility was hit in the Russian attack, warning that some areas of the capital could experience disruptions to electricity and water supplies.

Klitschko did not specify which facility was damaged or where it was located.

In Kharkiv, a drone struck a nine-story residential building in the city's Kyivskyi District, damaging its top two floors. Two women, aged 43 and 68, suffered acute stress reactions as a result of the attack, Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Syniehubov said in a Telegram post.

Russian attacks across Ukraine killed 10 people and injured another 55 over past day.

As temperatures have dropped across Ukraine, Russian forces have intensified their attacks on the country's energy infrastructure.

Damage to energy facilities has forced Ukraine to halt electricity exports, while electricity imports have surged to their highest daily level since mid-June.

Since September, Russia has carried out more than 1,000 attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting not only power plants but also high-voltage substations and transmission lines, according to the Center for Economic Strategy (CES).
